chunks: Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-'Amraki, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far, who said:

I asked him about a woman wearing a bracelet and an armlet on part of her forearm, and she does not know whether the water runs beneath them or not—what should she do when she performs wudu (ablution) or ghusl (ritual bath)? He said: He said, “She should move it until she causes the water to enter beneath it, or remove it.” And regarding a tight ring, when one does not know whether the water runs beneath it during wudu (ablution) or not—what should he do? He said: “If he knows that the water does not enter beneath it, then he should remove it when he performs wudu (ablution).”

Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: It does not harm the one performing wudu (ablution) if some of the water that has fallen to the ground or elsewhere then falls upon his clothes and body; rather, it is tahir (ritually pure). Likewise, what falls upon pure ground from the water with which one performs istinja', then returns onto him, does not harm him and does not render anything of his clothes or body najis (ritually impure), unless it falls upon visible najasah (ritual impurity) and carries it back when it returns to him; then in that case it is obligatory upon him to wash whatever of it was affected.

key_terms.تُحَرِّكُهُ: she moves it so that water can reach beneath it
key_terms.نَجَاسَةٍ ظَاهِرَةٍ: visible ritual impurity that, if carried by water, causes contamination
key_terms.ٱلدُّمْلُجُ: an armlet or bangle worn on the forearm
key_terms.ٱلسِّوَارُ: a bracelet worn on the arm that may obstruct water from reaching the skin
key_terms.ٱلْخَاتَمِ: a ring that may be tight enough to block water

ai.seo_question: What should a person do in wudu (ablution) or ghusl (ritual bath) if a ring or bracelet may prevent water from reaching the skin?
ai.summary: This hadith gives legal rulings about ensuring water reaches the skin during wudu (ablution) and ghusl (ritual bath) when jewelry may block it. It also clarifies that splashed water remains tahir (ritually pure) unless it contacts visible najasah (ritual impurity) and carries that impurity back.
